Approach 1: Direct Correlation & Approach 1 directly relates matched in vitro and in vivo time points after preprocessing. The fitted model is then used as a time-scaling function that maps an in vitro time to a predicted in vivo time.

This approach can be useful when the two datasets have matching time points, or when interpolation can create matched pairs, and the main question is how in vitro time corresponds to in vivo time. & Double Exponential, Exponential, Linear, Linear (zero intercept), Power \\
Approach 2: Independent Model Fitting & Approach 2 fits the same model family separately to the in vitro and in vivo datasets. With fitting data alone, the report summarizes the two fitted models and their fitted-curve uncertainty. When prediction data are supplied, predictions can be generated by comparing the fitted in vivo and in vitro responses or by comparing fitted characteristic time constants when those values are available.

This approach can be useful when the two datasets were measured on different time schedules, when each dataset is expected to follow the same type of degradation curve, or when a specific model form is scientifically meaningful for both datasets. & Double Exponential, Exponential, Mass Loss (Gompertz), Mass Loss (One-Phase), Mass Loss (Surface Erosion), Mass Loss (Two-Phase), Power, Stretched Exponential \\
Approach 3: Direct Mapping & Approach 3 uses direct interpolation-based mappings between datasets rather than fitting a parametric model. It can describe value-ratio behavior over time and time-ratio behavior over value ranges. When prediction data are supplied, those mappings can be used to scale prediction values or prediction times.

This approach can be useful for exploratory comparisons, for datasets where a simple equation does not describe the observed pattern well, or when the user wants a direct data-based mapping rather than a fitted model. & No parametric model selection \\
